pharm: Selectively blocks beta-1 adrenergic receptors, reducing heart rate, contractility, and renin release.
quick: Hypertension/angina: 50 mg once daily, up to 100 mg/day
May be taken without regard to food
Avoid; may cause fetal harm (growth restriction, bradycardia)
Excreted in milk; monitor infant for bradycardia/hypoglycemia
Reduce dose; accumulates in renal impairment
Heart rate, blood pressure, signs of heart failure
summary: Atenolol is a cardioselective (beta-1) beta-blocker used to treat hypertension and angina pectoris and to reduce mortality after acute myocardial infarction. It is hydrophilic and predominantly renally eliminated, so the dose must be reduced in renal impairment. It should not be stopped abruptly.
indications: Hypertension, alone or with other antihypertensives
Long-term management of angina pectoris due to coronary atherosclerosis
Management of acute myocardial infarction to reduce cardiovascular mortality

dosage.d: Initial 50 mg once daily; increase to 100 mg once daily if needed
dosage.n: Doses above 100 mg/day add little benefit

dosage.d: Initial 50 mg once daily; increase to 100 mg once daily
dosage.n: Some patients need 200 mg once daily

dosage.d: Per protocol IV then oral; typically 50 mg twice daily or 100 mg once daily
CrCl 15-35: max 50 mg/day; CrCl <15: max 25 mg/day or 50 mg every other day

admin: Take at the same time each day, with or without food
Do not discontinue abruptly; taper over 1-2 weeks to avoid rebound angina/ischemia
Check heart rate and blood pressure before dosing if bradycardia or hypotension is a concern
moa: Atenolol competitively and selectively blocks beta-1 adrenergic receptors in the heart, decreasing heart rate, AV conduction, myocardial contractility, and cardiac output, and reducing renin release. These effects lower blood pressure and myocardial oxygen demand. Beta-1 selectivity is relative and diminishes at higher doses.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to atenolol or formulation components

preg: May cause fetal harm including intrauterine growth restriction, fetal bradycardia, and hypoglycemia; generally avoided, especially in the second and third trimesters. Use only if benefit clearly outweighs risk.
lact: Atenolol is excreted in human milk and may accumulate in the infant; monitor the breastfed infant for bradycardia, hypotension, and hypoglycemia, or consider alternatives.
renal: Atenolol is eliminated mainly unchanged by the kidneys and accumulates in renal impairment; reduce dose and frequency based on creatinine clearance.
hepatic: Minimal hepatic metabolism; no dosage adjustment needed in hepatic impairment.

major: Clonidine (risk of severe rebound hypertension if either is withdrawn; withdraw clonidine last)
moderate: Antiarrhythmics (e.g., amiodarone, disopyramide; additive myocardial depression)
interactions.food: May be taken without regard to meals.
interactions.diagnostics: May mask tachycardia of hypoglycemia or hyperthyroidism.

monitoring: Signs and symptoms of heart failure
counsel: Do not stop the medicine suddenly; abrupt withdrawal can worsen angina or trigger a heart attack
May cause tiredness, cold hands/feet, or dizziness on standing
Diabetics: be aware it can mask a fast heartbeat from low blood sugar
Report shortness of breath, swelling, or a very slow pulse
Take at the same time each day
pk: Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); protect from light/moisture
pearls: Hydrophilic and renally cleared; reduce dose in renal impairment
Low lipid solubility means fewer CNS side effects than lipophilic beta-blockers
Never stop abruptly in coronary disease
Beta-1 selectivity is dose-dependent and lessens at higher doses
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip it. Do not double up.
overdose: Presents with bradycardia, hypotension, heart failure, and bronchospasm. Treat with atropine for bradycardia, IV fluids and vasopressors for hypotension, glucagon, and IV beta-agonists or a pacemaker as needed. Atenolol is removed by hemodialysis.
